name: Olga Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We aren't tied to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the second-fix crew on a social housing scheme on the edge of town, forty-two flats in three-storey timber-frame blocks. Second fix means everything after the walls are boarded: stairs, doors, skirting, kitchens, the bits people actually touch. I start at seven with a walk-round and a snag list, then I'm hanging doors myself most of the morning because I'm still the fastest at it. Afternoons it's chasing deliveries and checking my four carpenters haven't scribed a worktop the wrong way round.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love handing over a flat to a family who's been on the waiting list for six years. Last month a woman cried at the front door because her kids would each have a bedroom. What wears me out is the paperwork and the deliveries, the kitchen units turning up in the wrong colour, that kind of thing. I've started using one of those AI chat apps now and then to write the snag emails, because my niece showed me and it saves me half an hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first one. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say, well, there you go, it writes my snag emails and that's about it. At work it'd be a shrug and a joke at break. I don't really post online, except pictures of finished stairs in the trade group.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be a little bit disappointed, because I'd hoped it would take the boring paperwork off people like me. But mostly I'd think good, the building money can go on building and not on gadgets. Housing is what this town needs, not robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carry on. I'd keep using the chat app for emails when I remember, keep running the crew, keep putting money aside for Amira's school trip and the boiler. Karim and I would keep doing what we do, which is overpaying the mortgage a little when there's a good month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, really. Same as now, which is busy but fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's one thing you'd still want AI to take off you, even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Chasing deliveries. I spend an hour a day on the phone to the merchant asking where the door linings are. If a computer could just sort that out properly, I'd hug it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the money should go on building. Who decides that, as you see it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The council and the housing association, mostly, and the government that funds them. When they're short, they cut the number of flats, not the number of consultants. That's my real grumble, and it has nothing to do with AI.

S0.say: She'd shrug at work and say AI writes her snag emails and that's all. She doesn't post much, apart from photos of finished stairs in a trade group.
S0.think: Privately she'd be a little disappointed it didn't take more paperwork off her. Mostly she'd be glad money goes into housing rather than gadgets, because housing is what her town needs.
S0.do: Carries on running the second-fix crew and using a chat app for emails now and then. Keeps saving for the boiler and her daughter's school trip and overpays the mortgage in good months.
S0.feel: Calm, busy but fine, much the same as today.
S0.quote: If a computer could just sort that out properly, I'd hug it.
S0.fieldNote: Olga's pride is in handing over homes to families, and her politics run through public housing funding. She already uses AI a little, only because someone she trusts showed her. Her real complaints are deliveries and funding cuts, not technology.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's coming, so let's make sure the people building the homes get trained, not just the managers. In the trade group I'd ask who's actually tried the new tools and what they're like, because I'm not buying anything on the say-so of a salesman.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us, I don't think it touches my hands much. Hanging a door in an old frame that's out of square, no machine's doing that soon. But the factory-made walls are already coming in, and if whole bathrooms arrive as pods, my crew shrinks from four to two, and I'd have to choose who goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait until a couple of the other site leads had tried the scheduling apps, then I'd use whatever worked for them. I'd ask the company to pay for a short course in reading the new digital drawings, because that's what's actually coming. Money-wise, nothing big, we've got about eight months saved and that's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. A bit of a knot about my crew, but not about me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If your crew went from four to two, who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Petra. She's fifty-eight, brilliant on stairs, can't stand phones. The young ones would find something, there's work everywhere round here. Petra would just go quiet and leave, and that'd be a loss for everyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait until others tried the tools. Why not go first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I've seen three different apps come and go on our sites. The first one lost a whole week of my hours. I'll go second, happily, but I'm not paying the price of being first.

S1.say: She'd say at work that the people actually building homes need training, not just managers. Online she'd ask other trades who has really tried the new tools before trusting a sales pitch.
S1.think: Privately she doesn't think machines can do fiddly finish work soon. She worries more about factory pods shrinking her crew from four to two and having to choose who goes.
S1.do: Waits for other site leads to test scheduling apps, then adopts what works for them. Asks the company to fund a short course on digital drawings and leaves her eight months of savings untouched.
S1.feel: Calm about herself, with a small knot of worry about her crew.
S1.quote: I'll go second, happily, but I'm not paying the price of being first.
S1.fieldNote: Steady through and through: she wants proof from peers before she moves. Her concern goes to a specific older colleague, Petra, which says a lot about how she leads. She frames training as something employers owe workers, in line with her politics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need the government to treat this like a war or a pandemic, with wages protected while people work out what's next. At work I'd be pushing everyone to join the union, even the ones who think it's old-fashioned. Online I'd probably post more than I ever have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be scared, but not frozen. Karim's a maths teacher, and if AI can do almost any work, I don't know if they'll still pay a person to stand in front of thirty teenagers. Two years is our scheme finishing and maybe one more, and then I don't know who's hiring a carpenter at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: First month, Karim and I would sit at the kitchen table with the bank statements and stop the extension plan for good. We'd keep the eight months saved and try to stretch it to a year. I'd join the union properly, not just pay the dues, and go to the meetings with the housing association. I'd also start asking around about who's training people to look after the robots, but I wouldn't jump on anything until I'd talked to someone who'd done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Tight in the chest, but I've got a list, and lists help me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Amira and Yusuf?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The truth, but the gentle version. Amira's fourteen, she reads the news, she'd know anyway. I'd tell her we have money saved, we have a house, and Mum and Dad are good at working things out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think should pay for this?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies that sell the robots and the ones that save the wages. If my company saves my salary, some of it should go back to me while I find my feet. That's not a handout, that's just fair.

S2.say: She'd call for the government to treat it like an emergency and protect wages while people adjust. At work she'd push everyone to join the union, and she'd post online more than ever.
S2.think: Privately she fears both her job and her husband's teaching job could go within two years. She'd be scared but not frozen, and unsure who would hire a carpenter once the current scheme ends.
S2.do: Sits down with her husband in the first month, cancels the extension plan and tries to stretch eight months of savings to a year. Becomes an active union member and asks around about robot maintenance training, but only acts after talking to someone who's done it.
S2.feel: Anxious and tight in the chest, but steadied by having a list.
S2.quote: If my company saves my salary, some of it should go back to me while I find my feet. That's not a handout, that's just fair.
S2.fieldNote: Even under a fast shock she keeps her steady habit of checking with someone who's done it first. Her strong savings and organised temperament hold her at anxious rather than alarmed. Her fairness argument is clear and personal, framed around her own wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is our chance to plan it properly. At the union I'd want a training fund that workers can use while still on pay. In the trade group I'd start a thread on what people are actually doing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, five years feels like enough to make one real change. By then a few people will have done the robot supervisor courses, and I'll know if they were any good. That's how I like to do it, let someone else find the potholes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For the first couple of years I'd keep working and put an extra two hundred a month aside. Around year two or three, once I'd seen how the first lot of people got on, I'd sign up for whatever retraining worked, probably site robotics or inspection. We'd also look at Amira's university plans and maybe steer her away from anything too easy to automate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. More like a long to-do list than a fire alarm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What changes for you between two years and five?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years, I'm reacting. Five years, I'm choosing. The difference is I get to watch other people try first, and that's worth a lot to someone like me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Petra to do in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retire, honestly, with dignity and a decent pension. She's earned it. I'd want the union to fight for early pensions for people like her, not push them into a classroom with a laptop.

S3.say: She'd tell her union and trade group that five years is a chance to plan properly. She'd want a training fund that workers can use while still being paid.
S3.think: Privately she feels five years is enough for one real change, especially once others have tested the courses. She likes letting someone else find the potholes first.
S3.do: Keeps working and saves an extra two hundred a month for the first two years. Signs up for proven retraining in site robotics or inspection around year two or three, and rethinks her daughter's university plans.
S3.feel: Uneasy, like a long to-do list rather than a fire alarm.
S3.quote: Two years, I'm reacting. Five years, I'm choosing.
S3.fieldNote: For Olga, the extra time matters because it lets others go first, which is exactly how she adapts. She'd retrain, but on a schedule set by other people's results. She keeps thinking about Petra and wants early pensions for older workers rather than forced retraining.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one's called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's no excuse for anyone to be caught out, and I'd say it loudly to the council and the housing association. Ten years is time to train a whole generation differently. At work I'd be the one pushing for apprentices to learn the new kit alongside the old.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me fifty-three. I'd have done my best years in the trade, and I could see myself teaching carpentry at the college for a while. Whether colleges still have human teachers by then, I honestly don't know.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep leading the crew for five or six years and save steadily. Around year five I'd start teaching evening classes at the college to see if I liked it, because that's a low-risk way to test it. We'd overpay the mortgage so it's nearly done by 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but the soft kind. There's time to breathe and look around.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Yusuf, who'd be twenty by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell him to learn a trade and something else, maybe how the machines work. And to be kind to people, because I think that's what's left when the machines do the rest. He'd roll his eyes, he's ten and already rolls his eyes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Earlier you said a machine can't hang a door in a frame that's out of square. Do you still think so in ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if I'm honest. In ten years they'll manage it. I just like believing it a bit longer, because it's the part of the job I'm proudest of.

S4.say: She'd tell the council and housing association loudly that nobody should be caught out with ten years' warning. At work she'd push for apprentices to learn new machines alongside traditional skills.
S4.think: Privately she sees herself at fifty-three moving into teaching carpentry at the college. She admits she doesn't know if colleges will still have human teachers by then.
S4.do: Keeps leading the crew for five or six years while saving steadily and overpaying the mortgage. Starts evening teaching at the college around year five as a low-risk test of a second career.
S4.feel: Mildly uneasy, with time to breathe and look around.
S4.quote: I just like believing it a bit longer, because it's the part of the job I'm proudest of.
S4.fieldNote: With a decade she builds a gentle, tested path into teaching. Her honest admission about the door-hanging point was striking: she knows her belief is partly comfort. She keeps tying the future to how people treat each other, not just to skills.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because both Karim and I could be hit at once and there'd be nobody ahead of us to learn from. What would help is a wage that carries on while you retrain, paid for by the companies that save money on us. And real advice from people who've done it, not a leaflet.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the families we build for. If everybody's out of work, who pays the rent on these flats? I'd hate to build forty-two homes and have half of them sitting empty because nobody's got a wage.

headlineQuote: Hanging a door in an old frame that's out of square, no machine's doing that soon.
portrait: Olga Ibrahim is a 43-year-old second-fix lead carpenter on a social housing scheme, married to a maths teacher, with a daughter of fourteen and a son of ten. She uses AI now and then for emails, but only after someone she trusts has shown her, and she always prefers to go second. She stays calm through the plateau and steady change, grows anxious when AGI arrives in two years and threatens both incomes, and uses longer warnings to retrain only once others have proven a course. Her politics show in her call for companies that save wages to fund workers' retraining.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028 worries her most, because she and her husband could both lose work with nobody ahead of them to learn from.
whatWouldHelp: A wage that continues during retraining, paid for by the companies that save on labour, and real advice from people who've already made the change.
